rv.q: There’s a moment in Arcadia when Thomasina Coverly, the 13-year-old genius at the heart of Tom Stoppard’s great, humane play, laments the burning of the ancient library in Alexandria and, with it, so much learning. “How can we sleep for grief?” she cries to her tutor, Septimus.
Cracknell's stellar Old Vic revival ditches the rolling lawns and airy Classical architecture of Stoppard's setting in favour of a fluid, dimly lit, in-the-round staging
The sparky banter between these two pairs perfectly encapsulates the dramatic tensions that make Stoppard’s writing so compelling.
Major rising star Isis Hainsworth is phenomenal as Thomasina.
Carrie Cracknell’s production delivers considerable lucidity but without wings.
It’s like a complicated piece of algebra, exquisite in its difficulties, unsolvable to the end.

Stripped of all décor, the play appears ever more daunting and ever less dramatic and in the underpowered first half of Carrie Cracknell’s production the atmosphere falls dangerously flat.
Carrie Cracknell's magnificent revival has huge amounts of humour and heart, which is not always a given with Stoppard's work.

There is an unbridled joy in hearing Stoppard’s intelligence and wordcraft delivered by a troupe of universally accomplished players, so it is perhaps surprising that this is the first London revival of ARCADIA since 2009.

On that very point, I doubt this particular work will soon find a staging to match the empathic reach of Carrie Cracknell's altogether resplendent Old Vic revival, which manages the impossible, at least for me.
Serious, playful, teasing, Arcadia is pure alchemy, turning erudition and research into theatrical gold.
Cracknell delivers superbly on Stoppard’s classic.

Even if at points he’s guilty of wearing his learning a little too heavily, and the running time of nearly three hours feels indulgent, Stoppard nevertheless drops pearl after pearl of linguistic brilliance throughout.
But the self-conscious intellectualism of the 33-year-old play itself now feels decidedly dated.
The density of the writing, the complexity of the ideas, the lecture-like feel of far too many monologues and the bewildering cast of characters make it an ordeal rather than a joy.

cn.t: Cracknell's resplendent revival of Stoppard's masterpiece dazzles with humor and heart, though its dense intellectual complexity occasionally exhausts. Critics mostly praise the production's emotional resonance and wit.
